summary:
Article 567 of the Penal Code criminalises sexual relations with a person of the same sex and applies to conduct by both men and women. It was passed on 22 November 2008 and took effect on 22 April 2009; such conduct was not criminalised before that date. The penalty is three months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 100,000 Burundian francs. Reporting by OutRight International as of March 2026 cites Article 250 of the Penal Code for the same offence, with up to two years in prison and a fine; the article number differs from the 2008 provision and the sources do not reconcile the two.

Burundi provides no legal gender recognition as of March 2026, so a visitor cannot obtain local documents or markers matching their gender, and LGBTIQ organisations cannot register as associations.

Article 29 of the Constitution bans same-sex marriage, and Burundi recognises neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition for a spouse or partner.

In December 2023 President Évariste Ndayishimiye said homosexuals found in Burundi should be taken to stadiums and stoned, and rejected development aid conditioned on respect for LGBT rights. Human Rights Watch called on the ruling party to renounce persecution. The Iteka League, a Burundian human rights organisation working in exile, described the remarks as a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people, and members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described them as a real license to kill.

Arrests are documented while prosecutions of consensual adult conduct rarely reach conviction. On 1 July 2009 a man in Bujumbura was arrested for being gay and police sought money in exchange for his release before advocacy secured it. In 2012 two lesbians were briefly arrested and released. In September 2014 a case in Karuzi Province involving a Viettel employee and a Burundian man was dropped after three days for lack of evidence. Reporting for 2016 recorded no prosecutions during that year.

The one recorded conviction attached to a same-sex charge, on 2 November 2016 at the High Court of Cibitoke Province, sentenced a 15-year-old boy to one year in prison on charges of rape of a minor and homosexuality, following his admission of raping a seven-year-old boy.

In March 2023 twenty-four people were arrested on same-sex conduct charges; one of the accused died in detention; the group was acquitted on the conduct charge and seven were convicted of inciting debauchery. In August 2023 seven people were sentenced to one to two years in prison for homosexual acts.

United States State Department human rights reports from 2009 through 2016 list discrimination against gay and lesbian people among the country's common abuses, alongside torture, extrajudicial executions, arbitrary detention and media shutdowns, and record societal discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity without government protection. OutRight International describes extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances, arbitrary arrests, torture and sexual and gender-based violence with no meaningful legal reform. These conditions determine what protection, medical care and custody conditions a detained visitor can expect; the inventory contains no general homicide rate for Burundi, so no comparison between general and trans-specific violence levels can be made.
tangentialFactors:
International pressure has limited purchase. President Ndayishimiye rejected development aid conditioned on respect for LGBT rights in December 2023, and the response of Human Rights Watch was an appeal to the ruling party to renounce persecution rather than a claim of legal leverage. The most direct public criticism of the remarks came from the Iteka League, a Burundian human rights organisation working in exile, and from LGBTQ associations whose members could speak only anonymously.

Enforcement patterns shifted in 2023. Through 2016 the documented record was of arrests and short detentions that ended without prosecution of consensual adult conduct; in March 2023 a mass arrest of twenty-four people ended in acquittal on the conduct charge but seven convictions for inciting debauchery following a death in detention, and in August 2023 seven people received prison terms of one to two years for homosexual acts.
localsOnly:
LGBTIQ organisations cannot register, which removes the formal channel through which residents could organise, seek funding or press for legal change. There is no legal gender recognition, so identity documents, employment records and access to services follow the sex assigned at birth.

Residents face discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity without government protection, and reporting records high levels of harassment, family rejection and stigmatisation. United States State Department human rights reports for 2009, 2010, 2012, 2015 and 2016 list discrimination against gay and lesbian people among the country's routine abuses.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penal code article number is not settled in the sources: the 2008 provision is cited as Article 567, while OutRight International's March 2026 country page cites Article 250 with the same penalty range. No source explains the discrepancy or whether the code was renumbered.

Human rights reporting in the inventory records extrajudicial killings and one death in detention in the March 2023 case, but gives no general homicide rate for Burundi, so no baseline comparison is possible, and no count of violence against trans people specifically is available.

Nothing in the inventory describes border, visa or airport screening practice: whether document markers or presentation are flagged on entry, whether secondary screening occurs, or whether trans travellers face questioning is not sourced.

No information covers bathroom or single-sex facility rules. Beyond the absence of legal gender recognition, no data addresses medical or care access specific to trans people.

Enforcement data is sparse: the documented cases span 2009 to 2023, no prosecution figures for recent years are given, and nothing distinguishes enforcement against trans people from enforcement against same-sex conduct generally.
